questions.q: Why does Castellan Retail's perimeter firewall use three interfaces (WAN, DMZ, Internal) instead of two?
options: Three interfaces are required by law for any firewall handling e-commerce traffic
It doubles the firewall's internet bandwidth
It has no real purpose — two interfaces would work identically
So one device can enforce the boundary between zones that don't deserve equal trust, instead of treating the public web server and internal data the same
questions.explain: The three-legged design lets one firewall enforce different trust levels for WAN, DMZ, and internal traffic instead of lumping the DMZ in with the internal network.

questions.q: Why does the public order-tracking web server belong in the DMZ instead of on the internal network behind a firewall rule?
options: Firewall rules can't protect internal servers at all, so location doesn't matter
DMZ placement makes the web server load faster for customers
The DMZ is simply a backup location in case the internal network goes down
A server reachable from the internet is assumed reachable by an attacker eventually, so it needs to sit where compromise doesn't give direct access to internal resources
questions.explain: The DMZ isolates public-facing servers so that even full compromise doesn't hand an attacker a direct path to payroll data, HR records, or the domain controller.

questions.q: What makes the DMZ-to-internal rule in this lab narrower than a typical "DMZ subnet to internal subnet" rule?
options: It allows unlimited traffic between the two zones as long as it's encrypted
It only applies during business hours
It blocks all traffic between the DMZ and internal network with no exceptions at all
It's scoped to one specific host talking to one specific host on one specific port, not whole subnets
questions.explain: Host-to-host, single-port scoping means a compromised web server can only reach the one database host on the one port it was ever allowed to reach — not the entire internal VLAN.

questions.q: Why does Guest Wi-Fi get its own VLAN with a deny rule to internal VLANs, rather than just a Wi-Fi password?
options: Guest Wi-Fi doesn't need any security controls since it's for visitors only
VLANs are only used for performance, not security, in this design
Because a password controls who joins the network, not what that device can reach once it's on — isolation prevents any route to internal assets regardless of credentials
A password is sufficient because guest devices are automatically untrusted by the firewall
questions.explain: A password is an authentication control; VLAN isolation with an explicit deny is what actually prevents a guest device from reaching internal VLANs even if it had valid credentials.

questions.q: In this lab's internal VLAN design, why are Workstations and Servers placed on separate VLANs instead of one shared internal network?
options: Separate VLANs have no security benefit here — it's purely a naming convention
Because Windows requires workstations and servers to be on different VLANs to function
So a compromised workstation isn't one hop away from the domain controller or internal database
To reduce the total number of IP addresses needed
questions.explain: Segmenting workstations from servers limits how far an attacker who compromises one workstation can move laterally toward higher-value server assets.
